reference.source: Williams Hematology / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: The commonest of the rare inherited coagulation factor deficiencies, inherited in an autosomal recessive manner from F7 mutations
Characteristically causes an isolated prolonged prothrombin time with a normal activated partial thromboplastin time, because factor VII is the sole factor of the extrinsic pathway
The correlation between factor VII activity and bleeding severity is poor, so phenotype must guide management rather than the level alone
Clinical severity ranges from asymptomatic to serious bleeding, including mucocutaneous, joint, and, in severe cases, intracranial or gastrointestinal haemorrhage
Menorrhagia is a frequent presenting feature in affected women
Some patients experience thrombosis, and there is a recognised paradoxical thrombotic risk that complicates replacement therapy

Diagnosis rests on a specific factor VII activity assay after finding an isolated prolonged prothrombin time, with treatment using factor VII replacement (including recombinant factor VIIa) for bleeding or surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Factor VII is a vitamin K-dependent clotting factor that, on exposure to tissue factor at a site of vascular injury, initiates the extrinsic (tissue-factor) pathway of coagulation and triggers thrombin generation. Congenital deficiency, usually from biallelic mutations in F7, reduces the amount or function of the protein, so extrinsic pathway activation is impaired. Because factor VII participates only in the extrinsic limb, its deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time while leaving the activated partial thromboplastin time normal. The clinical phenotype is notably variable and correlates poorly with the measured factor level, reflecting compensatory features of the coagulation network; some individuals with very low levels bleed little, whereas others bleed significantly, and a subset paradoxically develop thrombosis.
additionalDifferentials: Vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect (multiple factors affected)
Combined deficiency of vitamin K-dependent factors
additionalInvestigations: Specific factor VII activity assay to confirm the deficiency
Prothrombin time (prolonged) with a normal activated partial thromboplastin time
Mixing studies to distinguish deficiency from an inhibitor
Assays of other vitamin K-dependent factors to exclude combined deficiency
Liver function tests to exclude an acquired cause
F7 genetic testing where confirmation or counselling is needed
redFlags: Intracranial or gastrointestinal haemorrhage, which can occur in severe deficiency
Severe bleeding in a neonate or after surgery in an undiagnosed patient
Heavy menstrual bleeding causing symptomatic anaemia
Thrombotic complications, which may be precipitated by replacement therapy
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the bleeding phenotype rather than the factor level; many patients have a mild course, while those with severe deficiency are at risk of major bleeding but can usually be managed effectively with targeted factor VII replacement.
pitfalls: Predicting bleeding risk from the factor VII level, which correlates poorly with phenotype
Attributing an isolated prolonged prothrombin time to warfarin or liver disease without assaying factor VII
Overlooking the paradoxical thrombotic risk when giving replacement therapy
Failing to investigate menorrhagia as a manifestation in affected women
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Replacement with recombinant activated factor VII as the preferred agent for bleeding and surgical cover, guided by the bleeding phenotype rather than the factor level alone
Plasma-derived factor VII concentrate or prothrombin complex concentrate as alternatives, with fresh frozen plasma only if concentrates are unavailable
Antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding, menorrhagia and as an adjunct to replacement
Hormonal management of menorrhagia in affected women
Regular prophylaxis in severe deficiency or after serious bleeds such as intracranial haemorrhage
Cautious, individualised replacement mindful of the recognised paradoxical thrombotic risk
Haematology-led perioperative and peripartum planning, avoiding antiplatelet agents and NSAIDs, with genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance
